title: Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler
gist: Together AI found that its record-setting megakernels were unproductizable and that default Torch Inductor kernels plus CUDA Graphs and PDL recover 98% of their performance; heterogeneous models and hardware make monolithic fusion suboptimal. It replaced rule-based compilation with a minimal agent-driven optimizer (Together Compiler) after learning that heavy scaffolding (IRs, knowledge hubs, expert strategies) hurt agents, claiming up to 1.7x over megakernels and up to 2.6x over optimized baselines.

themes.theme: Megakernels deleted: simple primitives match them

insights.claim: Together AI's hand-built Llama 1B megakernel reached 990 TPS on H100 (48% over Torch Inductor's 669 TPS), but after months of production work in late 2025 it supported only one model, one batch size (1), one precision (BF16) and one customer.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Record-breaking monolithic kernels can be commercially unproductizable; discount benchmark-only inference speed claims that lack workload flexibility.
insights.quote: we had a grand total of one model, one batch size, and one customer.
insights.locator: Introduction / Then we tried putting megakernels into production

insights.claim: Default Torch Inductor kernels plus CUDA Graphs and fine-grained Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL) reach 975 TPS on Llama 1B H100, 98% of the hand-optimized megakernel, without writing a single custom kernel.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Much of the 'custom kernel' performance moat in inference is replicable with stock NVIDIA primitives, compressing differentiation for kernel-specialist startups.
insights.quote: we could recover 98% of megakernel performance without writing a single kernel
insights.locator: Putting all of this together, default PyTorch Inductor kernels

insights.claim: Stepwise ablation on Llama 1B H100: Torch Compile 669 TPS, +CUDA Graphs 864 TPS (87% of megakernel), +PDL 953 TPS (96%), +fine-grained PDL placement 975 TPS (98%).
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Launch-overhead removal is the dominant lever in small-batch decode; CUDA Graphs alone captures most of the gain.
insights.locator: Launch overhead. Kernel launch overhead is costly.

insights.claim: In PyTorch, ATen dispatch costs 37 microseconds for an H100 Llama 1B down-projection whose GPU execution is only 15 microseconds; even pure C++ launches cost about 2 microseconds each, adding up across hundreds of kernels per forward pass.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: CPU-side framework overhead, not GPU FLOPs, often bounds low-latency decode—favoring graph capture and host-side optimization tooling.
insights.quote: Thirty-seven microseconds of paperwork for fifteen microseconds of work
insights.locator: Launch overhead.

insights.claim: Megakernels do not eliminate launch costs; they trade them for in-kernel synchronization: megakernel grid sync costs 646 ns on H100 vs 645 ns for CUDA Graph + PDL, while a normal cudaLaunchKernelEx costs 2,077 ns (2,496 ns on B200).
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: The headline advantage of persistent megakernels is largely illusory once modern launch primitives are used.
insights.quote: it just trades launch overhead for similar synchronization costs inside the kernel
insights.locator: Synchronization cost across launch mechanisms on H100 and B200

insights.claim: Intra-kernel synchronization is slightly slower on NVIDIA B200 than H100 because B200 is split into two separate dies; single-die sync matches H100 for an equivalent SM count.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Multi-die GPU designs introduce sync penalties that favor software designs avoiding global grid barriers.
insights.locator: Interestingly, intra-kernel synchronization is slightly slower on B200

insights.claim: Compute-overlap benefits of persistent kernels are limited: in the Llama 1B H100 megakernel three of five producer-consumer edges per layer require full barriers (a fourth is effectively full), so only the attention instruction meaningfully benefits from overlap.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Inherent serialization in transformer layers caps gains from exotic scheduling; skepticism warranted toward persistent-kernel marketing.
insights.locator: Compute overlap. Wave quantization occurs

insights.claim: Megakernel paged-memory weight preloading was worth only about 3.3% of forward time (990 to 961 TPS when removed), and PDL with carefully placed griddepcontrol.wait recovers up to 98% of that gain.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Memory-prefetch tricks are second-order in decode; simpler tooling captures them.
insights.quote: Memory preloading helps, but not a lot
insights.locator: Memory overlap. Our earlier megakernel divided

themes.theme: Why monolithic kernels fail on new hardware/models

insights.claim: Megakernels force one launch envelope (warp count, registers, cluster shape) on all ops: Hopper wgmma GEMMs run best at 12 warps, and forcing them into the megakernel's 20-warp configuration makes them 1.2-1.5x slower; AMD hardware faces the same register constraint, though Blackwell's tcgen05 does not.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Hardware heterogeneity (NVIDIA generations plus AMD) structurally penalizes one-size kernel strategies, favoring adaptive compilers.
insights.locator: Persistent kernels force hardware tradeoffs

insights.claim: Packing a whole model into one megakernel binary overflows the SM instruction cache, causing evictions and refetches when operations repeat.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Another hidden cost of monolithic fusion that grows with model complexity.
insights.locator: Megakernels also add pressure to the SM's instruction cache

insights.claim: Kimi K3 on Blackwell interleaves KDA and MLA layers that need different tensor-core cta_group modes (single-CTA vs CTA-pair), which PTX forbids mixing in one kernel, so a megakernel cannot run both optimally.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Architectural diversity in frontier open models (hybrid attention, MoE) makes inference optimization a per-model problem—a moat for continual optimization services.
insights.quote: PTX forbids mixing these two different modes into one kernel
insights.locator: Modern architectures don't fit single envelopes

insights.claim: For Kimi K3, running MoE GEMMs tensor-parallel and attention projections data-parallel means TP GEMMs process 8x more tokens and need a different cluster size; forcing one cluster size causes a 5-19% slowdown.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Mixed parallelism schemes in production MoE serving reward per-op tuning.
insights.locator: During inference, different kernels may require different parallelism schemes

insights.claim: Un-fusing can win: moving Kimi K3 expert dispatch to the GPU copy engine beat Mixture of Kittens' MoE megakernel by 6.9% under imbalanced routing, and FlashInfer's MegaMoE ran 17% faster by factoring dispatch out of its GEMM.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Contrary to the 'fuse everything' consensus, the edge is choosing which ops to couple—a search problem suited to automated/agentic tuning.
insights.quote: Fusion for the sake of fusion is not always ideal.
insights.locator: Examining open source kernels, we found

themes.theme: Torch Inductor's heuristic and benchmarking gaps

insights.claim: Torch Inductor's 'freezing' flag improved throughput 10-26% at larger batch sizes but caused a 49% slowdown at batch size 1, because an FP32 weight conversion was not reversed for matrix-vector operations.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Static compiler heuristics can badly misfire on latency-critical batch-1 serving; workload-specific search has real value.
insights.locator: The best optimization depends on the workload.

insights.claim: As of Q3 2026 Torch Inductor exposes 607 tuning flags, 198 added in the past year, and their effects interact non-additively (aggressive_fusion alone cost 6 TPS on Llama 1B but combined with three other flags gained 3 TPS).
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: The exploding configuration space argues for systematic/agentic search over human-tuned compilers.
insights.quote: As of Q3 2026, Inductor exposes 607 tuning flags, 198 of which were added in the past year.
insights.locator: Optimizations interact in unpredictable ways.

insights.claim: Inductor's isolated kernel benchmarks flush L2 cache and include CPU launch idle time, overestimating kernel times by 39-58% versus live inference and reporting 2.5 µs for an op doing no GPU work; this led it to pick a Triton GEMM 15% slower than cuBLAS on Llama 1B's output projection.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Benchmark fidelity is a hidden performance lever; vendors measuring inside real forward passes gain edge.
insights.locator: Finding #2: The fastest kernel in isolation

insights.claim: Unrealistic benchmark inputs distort results: zero-initialized token IDs made torch.embedding 2.1x faster than random IDs at 64K tokens, and random inputs misjudged GLM 5.3's MoE grouped-GEMM latency by 4-21%.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Data-dependent architectures (MoE) make realistic-input profiling essential.
insights.quote: accurate benchmarking requires taking measurements from inside a real forward pass on real input data
insights.locator: Benchmark inputs can also distort cache behavior

insights.claim: Inductor's greedy pairwise fusion scores candidates by memory-traffic savings and so rejects fusing kernels sharing no memory, even when one launches just 6 CTAs leaving most of an H100's 132 SMs idle.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Fusion algorithms should optimize GPU utilization, not just memory traffic.
insights.quote: an algorithm for kernel fusion should reason about utilization, not just memory
insights.locator: Finding #3: Inductor leaves fusion opportunities on the table.

themes.theme: Agent-built kernels need real data and context

insights.claim: A static repository of pre-generated agent kernels swapped into Torch graphs proved ineffective because the best kernel depends on the model, workload and surrounding operations.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Kernel libraries/marketplaces have limited value vs in-context continual optimization.
insights.quote: a static registry could not easily account for this
insights.locator: In March when these experiments were taking place

insights.claim: An agent-written top-k indexer ran in 20 µs on random inputs but 62 ms on real inputs, because ReLU-produced exact zeros concentrated candidates into one histogram bin and triggered quadratic work.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: AI-generated kernels validated on synthetic data can catastrophically regress in production—a risk for agentic codegen vendors.
insights.quote: Agents need real data and full execution context to generate optimizations that hold up in production.
insights.locator: Furthermore, synthetic inputs misled agents.

insights.claim: Together AI found that by March coding agents had become remarkably capable at writing GPU kernels, shifting its approach from a rule-based compiler to an agent-centric compiler.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Frontier coding agents are now credible GPU kernel engineers, threatening scarce-human-expertise moats in CUDA optimization.
insights.quote: coding agents had become remarkably capable at writing GPU kernels
insights.locator: In March when these experiments were taking place

themes.theme: Bitter lessons: less scaffolding, better agents

insights.claim: Together AI's custom BlockIR (driver-level kernel capture via CUPTI/rocProf with symbolic pointer mapping) was abandoned because agents spent more time debugging pointer tracking than optimizing; agents now edit forward-pass source code directly.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: As frontier models improve, elaborate IRs become liabilities; simpler source-level agent loops win.
insights.quote: agents were spending more time debugging pointer tracking than identifying optimizations
insights.locator: Phase 1: Capturing a sequence of kernels

insights.claim: In Kimi K2.6 on TensorRT-LLM, 23 of 24 decoder-layer kernels are dispatched through C++ as custom torch ops and are opaque to Torch Inductor, limiting what PyTorch's FX graph compilers can optimize.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Production engines largely bypass PyTorch compilers, so compiler-level optimization tools must work beyond FX graphs.
insights.locator: We started from PyTorch's FX Graph IR.

insights.claim: Host-side optimizations outside kernel IRs matter: rewriting Kimi K3's MLA metadata planning to split long sequences across thread blocks sped the MLA kernel 1.7-2.5x.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Agentic optimizers with full source access can capture gains invisible to kernel-only compilers.
insights.locator: A limited optimization space.

insights.claim: On GLM 5.3 on AMD, clock drift up to 325 µs between launch hooks and PyTorch's allocator history mislabeled pointers, illustrating brittleness of pointer-level IR capture.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: AMD tooling paths remain rougher, adding friction for cross-vendor optimization.
insights.locator: Even identifying pointers in the first place was fragile.

insights.claim: An expert-curated knowledge hub made agents 25-31% worse by anchoring them to known patterns; on MiniMax-M3 layer 3 (B200, TP4, batch 1) it cut ensemble speedup from 5.85x to 4.75x.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Retrieval-augmented 'expert knowledge' can harm agent search—relevant to RAG/agent tooling vendors' value propositions.
insights.locator: Knowledge hub. Our system used a knowledge hub

insights.claim: A naive prompt to 'make this forward pass as fast as possible' outperformed six expert-written strategy ensembles (6.20x vs 4.92x, 26% better), as prescribing optimization order traps agents in local minima (phase-ordering problem).
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Human-prescribed workflows can cap agent performance; value shifts to measurement infrastructure and compute throughput.
insights.locator: Expert strategies. We initially seeded each parallel agent

insights.claim: Enforced DAG-style research logging consumed up to 43% of agents' CLI/tool calls per trial with little optimization value, so it was removed.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Agent bookkeeping overhead is a measurable tax; lean scaffolds improve compute efficiency.
insights.locator: Research and logging data structures.

insights.claim: Parallel agents communicating frequently via a lightweight message board reached 7.72x speedup vs 6.20x with infrequent and 4.82x with no communication, because isolation caused redundant duplicate work.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Multi-agent systems benefit from continuous coordination—a design signal for agent orchestration platforms.
insights.locator: Agent ensembling.

insights.claim: Systems built around agents should anticipate improving model capabilities, because scaffolding that helps early can later become a constraint.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Bet on minimal, measurement-centric agent infrastructure that scales with model progress rather than heavy bespoke frameworks.
insights.quote: frameworks that help early on can later become constraints
insights.locator: Wrapping Up

insights.claim: Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven continual inference optimizer, runs in under 24 hours on no more than two nodes and generates up to 1.7x higher TPS than Together's megakernel baseline (over 1,100 TPS for Llama 1B on H100).
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Together AI is productizing automated per-customer inference optimization as a differentiator vs other inference clouds; offered in early access.
insights.locator: This minimal system is what powers Together Compiler today.

insights.claim: Together Compiler claims to beat highly optimized baselines by up to 2.6x, setting low-latency state of the art at 1,111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1,205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and speedups up to 6.4x on open-source codebases in weather modeling, PDEs, time-series and biology.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: If generalizable, agentic optimization expands beyond LLM serving into scientific computing, widening Together AI's TAM; claims are vendor self-reported.
insights.quote: setting state-of-the-art low-latency performance with 1,111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1,205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash
insights.locator: Tops engine leaderboards

insights.claim: Together AI argues inference is becoming heterogeneous—new architectures weekly, shifting batch sizes and sequence lengths, proliferating hardware—so the winning approach is continual, workload-specific optimization rather than monolithic kernels or static compiler heuristics.
insights.speaker: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Hardware/model fragmentation increases value of optimization software layers and erodes single-vendor lock-in; watch inference providers' compiler moats.
insights.locator: Introduction / Wrapping Up

source_meta.author: Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora
